For the Proportions of the Yards of a Ship, they commonly allow J of the Length of her Keel, or of the Length of her Mainmast, for the Length of her Main-yards ; and for the Thick ness of them, they allow -J of an Inch for every Yard in Length ; the Top-yardis f of the Main-yard, andrheForcyard is J of the Main-yard, or as some say •*: The Sprirfail-yard and Cross-jack, are of the same Length, vi%. 7 the Missen-yard; and the Thickness of the Mislen-yard and Sprirfail-yard is 7 Inch to a Yard in Length. All small Yards are half the great Yards from Cleat to Cleat: when a great Yard is down a Portlast, it gives the Length of all Topfail-slieats, Lifts and Tics, Jeers and Bunt-lines; as also of the Leech-lines and Halliards, measuring from the Hounds to the Deck: And when it is Hoised, it gives the Length of Clew-lincs, Braces, Clew-garnets, Tackles, Sheats and Bow-lines. The Terms belonging to the Yards, arc, i. Top the Yards ; that is, make them hang even. The Clew-iines do most properly Top the Main and Fore-yards; but when the Top-fails are stowed, then the Topfail-sheats will Top them. i. Brace the Yard, i. e.
